newsitem.title: USA: Clinton wants compromise with Republicans on taxes.
newsitem.headline: Clinton wants compromise with Republicans on taxes.

text.p: In an effort to jump-start negotiations with congressional Republicans, President Bill Clinton unveiled a compromise plan on Monday to cut taxes by $85 billion over five years.
The U.S. House of Representatives and Senate by wide margins last week approved tax-cutting bills that follow the broad outlines of a balanced-budget deal between Congress and the White House.

Clinton and many Democrats say the Republican plans are skewed toward the affluent and are particularly unhappy with a House plan to index capital gains. The White House also wants assurances that low-income workers will be eligible for a child tax credit.
Following is a comparison of the House and Senate measures and the new White House proposal:
OVERALL LEVEL -- The House bill and Clinton's proposal would cut taxes by a net $85 billion over five years. The Senate bill includes $77 billion in tax reductions.

CAPITAL GAINS -- The House and Senate bills cut the top capital gains rate to 20 percent from 28 percent. The House indexes capital gains for inflation. Clinton opposes indexing, saying it would boost the amount of revenue loss in later years and make it difficult to keep the budget balanced.

The White House plan calls for a 30 percent exclusion on capital gains taxes for investments held over one year. Capital gains would not be indexed for inflation. It includes a $500,000 exclusion for capital gains on home sales for a couple, $250,000 for single filers and increases the existing exclusion for equity investment in small businesses.

TOBACCO TAXES -- The Senate bill would increase the federal cigarette tax by 20 cents per pack, with part of the proceeds going to expand health care for children. The House bill does not include a tobacco tax increase.
Clinton's plan calls for a 20-cents-per-pack increase to be put in a trust fund to expand children's health care.

CHILD TAX CREDIT -- The House and Senate generally provide a $500 per child credit for single taxpayers making up to $75,000 and couples with incomes up to $110,000. The credit applies to children up to age 17, with some differences.

The White House calls for a credit of $400 in 1998, $500 in 1999 and indexed thereafter. It would cover children under 17 through 2002 and up to 19 in later years. The credit would be phased out for families making $60,000-$75,000 until 2000 and then $80,000-$100,000 thereafter. It would be partially refundable against payroll taxes to aid lower-income workers.
ESTATE TAXES -- The House and Senate bills gradually raise the level of estates exempt from taxation to $1 million from the current $600,000.
Clinton's plan would exclude an additional $900,000 from estate taxes for family-owned farms and businesses. That change would shield the first $2.1 million from tax.

EDUCATION -- The House and Senate include tax credits for tuition and other expenses for higher education, call for tax-preferred education savings accounts and let taxpayers withdraw money from Individual Retirement Accounts for education expenses.

Clinton's plan includes two-year HOPE scholarships with a maximum credit of $1,500 a year beginning in 1998 and a 20 percent tuition tax credit for third and fourth year students, graduate students and working people who return to school.
It also allows penalty-free use of Individual Retirement Accounts for higher education and sets up Kidsave accounts.
